passages.t: A man with a long-lasting discharge
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron. “When any man has a bodily discharge, the discharge is unclean” (verse 2).

While it lasts, what he lies on, sits on or rides on is unclean (verses 4, 9). Anyone who touches his bed, his seat or his body “must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening” (verses 5-7). A clay pot he touches is broken, and a wooden one is rinsed (verse 12).

“When the man has been cleansed from his discharge, he must count off seven days for his cleansing, wash his clothes, and bathe himself in fresh water, and he shall be clean” (verse 13). On the eighth day he brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, who offers them. “In this way the priest will make atonement for the man before the LORD because of his discharge” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is the last of the chapters on clean and unclean. They have moved from food, to childbirth, to the skin, and now to the most private parts of bodily life. The chapter speaks frankly about the body, and it speaks without shame.

Two ideas have to be set aside before reading it.

The first is that unclean means sinful. Nothing in the chapter blames anyone. Uncleanness was a state a person was in for a time. It kept him from the sanctuary and from holy food. It ended with washing and waiting, and for a longer condition with an offering.

The second is that these laws are aimed at women. The chapter begins with men. It is built with care: a man's long-lasting discharge, then a man's ordinary emission, then husband and wife together at the center, then a woman's ordinary period, then a woman's long-lasting bleeding. The two long-term cases, his and hers, are treated in the same way: seven days, then the same offering of two birds.

The discharge in this first case is some kind of illness, probably an infection. The law does not treat it as a disgrace. It says how its uncleanness passes, by touch, to bed and seat and saddle, and how easily that is dealt with: wash, and wait for evening. The word ‘evening’ comes fifteen times in the chapter. Most of this uncleanness was brief, ordinary and soon over.

The offering at the end is the offering of the poor, two birds. No one is asked for a lamb.
passages.later:
The book of Numbers lists this with two other conditions that kept people outside the camp for a time: “anyone with a skin disease, anyone who has a bodily discharge, and anyone who is defiled by a dead body” (Numbers 5:2). It gives the reason: the camp is the place ‘where I dwell among them’ (Numbers 5:3).

Through Ezekiel God promised a cleansing that goes deeper than water: “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols” (Ezekiel 36:25).
passages.asks: The law spoke plainly about illness in the most private part of the body, and attached no shame to it. Ask whether there is a trouble in your body that you have been too ashamed to take to a doctor or to tell anyone about. And ask whether people near you could speak to you about such a thing without fear.

passages.happening:
“When a man has an emission of semen, he must bathe his whole body with water, and he will be unclean until evening” (verse 16). Any cloth or leather it touches is washed (verse 17).

“If a man lies with a woman and there is an emission of semen, both must bathe with water, and they will remain unclean until evening” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This short passage stands at the center of the chapter, and it shows better than any other what ‘unclean’ means in Leviticus.

A husband and wife who have slept together are unclean until evening. Yet marriage and children are gifts of God all through the Old Testament. The first command in the Bible is to be fruitful. So this uncleanness cannot be a mark of sin or of anything shameful. No offering is asked. They wash, and at sunset it is over.

Why, then, any uncleanness at all? Many scholars explain it in this way. Blood carries life, and seed carries the beginning of life. When either leaves the body, something of life is spent. Human life in the body is mortal. The God who lived in the tent is the God of life, who does not die. The laws kept a line between the two. Others add that keeping sex apart from worship set Israel off from religions in which sexual rites were part of what was done at a temple, though how common such rites really were in Canaan is debated.

The practical effect was simple. A couple did not go straight from their bed to the sanctuary. And every household in Israel lived with a daily sense that the holy God was near.
passages.later:
Genesis says of the first husband and wife, “And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25).

Before God came down on Mount Sinai, the people were told to make ready in the same way: “Do not draw near to a woman” (Exodus 19:15).

The letter to the Hebrews leaves no doubt about how marriage is to be regarded: “Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4).
passages.asks: The law called a married couple unclean until evening and never once called them guilty. Ask whether you carry shame about your body or about married love that God never put there. And ask how your home shows, in small daily ways, that God is near.

passages.happening:
“When a woman has a discharge consisting of blood from her body, she will be unclean due to her menstruation for seven days, and anyone who touches her will be unclean until evening” (verse 19).

What she lies or sits on in those days is unclean, and anyone who touches her bed or seat washes and is unclean until evening (verses 20-23). If a man lies with her and her flow touches him, “he will be unclean for seven days” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The same kind of rule that was given for men is now given for women. A woman's period made her unclean for seven days. In practice it meant that at regular times she did not go to the sanctuary. No offering is asked afterward. It was an ordinary thing, and time ended it.

The Hebrew word used here is niddah. Later prophets borrowed it as a picture for moral defilement. In this chapter it has no such meaning. It describes a natural state, with no blame.

The text gives its own reason for the whole chapter, and it has to do with the presence of God in the camp (verse 31). It has nothing to do with the worth of women.

It should also be said that the weight of these laws did not fall evenly. A monthly cycle meant that a woman was unclean more often than most men were. The hard question below faces that.
passages.later:
The prophets used this state as a picture of the nation's sin. Through Ezekiel God says of Israel, “Their behavior before Me was like the uncleanness of a woman’s impurity” (Ezekiel 36:17). The picture is about a people kept back from God's presence. It is not a judgment on women.

In the same chapter God promises to make that people clean himself (Ezekiel 36:25).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter treat women's bodies as shameful or dirty?

Many modern readers feel that it does, and the concern deserves a straight answer.

The chapter's own shape does not single women out. It begins with men, applies the same kind of rule to both, and sets man and woman together at its center. Uncleanness in Leviticus was not a moral judgment. It was shared by anyone who touched a dead body, had a skin disease, or slept with a husband or wife. A woman's period made her unclean for seven days. That was a state she was in, not a verdict on her.

It is also true that the effects were uneven. Her cycle meant more frequent uncleanness than most men knew. And later traditions sometimes widened these rules in ways that did push women to the edges. Readers disagree about how much of that pressure lies in the text and how much in its later use.

What the text states is its reason, in verse 31, and that reason is the presence of God, not the worth of women. The Gospels show Jesus welcoming a woman whose bleeding had kept her at the edges for twelve years.

So no one may use this chapter to shame a woman for her body, or to treat a girl's first period, or any period, as a disgrace. A word for anyone who has been made to feel unclean, by an illness, by your body or by your past. That is not what this book says of you. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law named a woman's monthly bleeding as an ordinary part of life and laid no guilt on it. Ask whether the women and girls you know are made to feel ashamed of their bodies, at home, at school or at church. And ask what you could say or do to lift that shame.

passages.t: Bleeding that does not stop, and the reason for it all
passages.happening:
“When a woman has a discharge of her blood for many days at a time other than her menstrual period, or if it continues beyond her period, she will be unclean all the days of her unclean discharge” (verse 25). Her bed and seat are unclean, as in her period (verses 26-27).

“When a woman is cleansed of her discharge, she must count off seven days, and after that she will be ceremonially clean” (verse 28). On the eighth day she brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons, and the priest makes atonement for her (verses 29-30).

Then the purpose of the whole chapter: “You must keep the children of Israel separate from their uncleanness, so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
This is the woman's case that matches the man's at the start of the chapter: an illness, a bleeding that goes on and on. It is treated just as his was. Seven days after it stops, and then the same small offering of two birds.

The offering does not mean she has sinned. As after childbirth, it is the purification offering. It marks her return to the sanctuary.

It is not hard to see how heavy this could be. A woman whose bleeding did not stop was unclean for as long as it lasted. That could be years. She could not go to the sanctuary, and whoever touched her became unclean for the day. The law gave her a way back when she was well. It could not make her well.

Verse 31 explains everything in chapters 11 to 15. God's tent is ‘among them’. Because he lives in the middle of the camp, the ordinary facts of bodily life have to be ordered around his presence. The warning is solemn: uncleanness carried carelessly into the tent is deadly. The next chapter gives the remedy. Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the tent itself is cleansed of all the uncleanness that has gathered around it, including what these laws could not catch.
passages.later:
Mark tells of exactly such a woman. “And a woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years” (Mark 5:25). By this chapter she had been unclean all that time. She came up behind Jesus in a crowd and touched his cloak. Her uncleanness did not pass to him. “Immediately her bleeding stopped” (Mark 5:29).

Jesus would not let her slip away unseen. He looked for her, and when she came forward, afraid, he said, “Daughter,” and then, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction” (Mark 5:34).

The letter to the Hebrews says that the way to God now stands open, and uses the language of washing: “let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22).
passages.asks: For twelve years a woman was kept at the edge of her people, and Jesus called her ‘Daughter’ in front of them all. Ask who near you lives with a long illness that keeps them from gathering with others. And ask how you, or your church, could go to them, and call them by a name that brings them in.
